# PicoCalc CPU Emulator

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

An old-computer emulator for the **ClockworkPi PicoCalc**, by **Thomas
Dzubin**, written in C against the **Raspberry Pi Pico SDK** and the
driver layer from
[`picocalc-text-starter`](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
by **Blair Leduc** (LCD and south-bridge keyboard drivers) — vendored here
under [`picocalc-text-starter-main/`](picocalc-text-starter-main/).

The eventual goal is to emulate different real or invented 8-bit
microprocessors, each with a 16-bit address space (8-bit bytes,
instructions 1 to 3 bytes long) — real architectures and completely
made-up ones alike. None of that exists yet. This is the first step only:
a way to get code and data into the emulated machine's memory in the
first place, before there's a CPU to run it, an assembler to write it in,
or a disassembler to read it back.

```
cpu_emulator.c                the whole program (for now)
cpu_emulator_config.h         every #define / tunable constant
CMakeLists.txt                builds the firmware, reusing picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/*
pico_sdk_import.cmake         standard Pico SDK locator (copied from the starter)
picocalc-text-starter-main/   vendored driver layer (see License; do not edit)
LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md         MIT licence; version history
```

## Where this stands

**Step 1: raw hexadecimal keyboard memory entry.** The emulator has a
full 64KB address space (`MEM[]`, one byte per address, `0x0000`-`0xFFFF`)
and a way to type hex straight into it from the keyboard. There is no CPU
definition, no instruction execution, and no assembly language yet — this
is purely a memory editor.

## Memory window

At power-up all 64KB of memory is filled with random bytes (0-255), so
there is something varied to browse.

The screen is a three-line window into memory. Each line is a row of 8
bytes: its address, the 8 bytes in hex, then the same 8 bytes as ASCII (a
period for anything not printable).

```
FFF8: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ........
0000: 4C F5 02 00 00 00 00 00 L.......
0008: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ........
```

The **cursor** byte is always on the middle line, outlined in white. The
line above and the line below are the neighbouring rows, so the window
moves with the cursor. Addresses wrap around: moving up from row `0000`
shows `FFF8`-`FFFF` on the middle line.

Above and to the right of the window, a larger square shows the cursor
byte in big digits, with an underline beneath the nibble the next hex
digit will fill in. The bottom line of the screen shows the cursor's
address.

To the left of the big square, level with its digits, the assembly
**mnemonic** for that byte is shown in large letters. It comes from a
256-entry instruction table (`INSTR[]`): for each possible opcode byte, a
mnemonic of up to five characters and the instruction's length in bytes.
For now every entry is `???` with a random length of 1 to 3 (chosen fresh
each power-up), except opcode `00`, which is `NOP` with length 1, until a
CPU is defined.

A 2-byte instruction also shows one argument after the mnemonic, and a
3-byte one shows two, in a smaller size on the same line. Until operands
are decoded, each argument is just `??`.

**Moving:** the left arrow moves the cursor back one byte; down and up
arrows move it a whole row (8 bytes). The right arrow moves forward by the
length of the instruction at the cursor (from the table), so it steps from
one instruction to the next.

**Entering bytes:** type a hex digit and it becomes the high nibble of the
cursor byte (shown in the big square, underline moving to the low nibble,
but not yet written to memory). The second digit completes the byte: it is
written to memory, shown in place for a quarter of a second so you can
check it, and then the cursor steps on to the next byte. Backspace
drops a half-typed nibble. Moving with an arrow key also drops it, leaving
the byte as it was.

**Jumping to an address:** ESC brings up an `ADDR> ` prompt on the bottom
line. Type up to four hex digits (backspace corrects), then ENTER moves the
cursor there, or press ESC again to cancel.

Any key that doesn't apply right now is rejected with a short beep and
otherwise ignored.

## Controls

| Key                    | Action                                      |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| 0-9, A-F (either case)  | type a hex digit (two complete a byte; four fill the ADDR> prompt) |
| RIGHT                   | cursor forward one instruction (its length from the table) |
| LEFT                    | cursor back one byte                          |
| DOWN / UP               | cursor forward / back one row (8 bytes)       |
| BACKSPACE               | drop a half-typed nibble (or a typed ADDR> digit) |
| ESC                     | open the ADDR> prompt; press again to cancel it |
| ENTER                   | at the ADDR> prompt, jump to that address     |
| Q                       | ask `EXIT AND LOSE MEMORY? Y/N` (the memory lives only in RAM); Y leaves for the PicoCalc UF2 Loader menu, anything else cancels |
| ~ (SHIFT + `)           | reboot into BOOTSEL (USB drive) mode          |

Leaving asks the loader for its menu through the watchdog scratch registers
(constants in `cpu_emulator_config.h`); if the program was flashed straight to
the chip with no loader installed it simply restarts.

## Building

VS Code Pico extension (Compile / Run), or from a terminal with
`PICO_SDK_PATH` set:

```
cmake -B build -G Ninja
ninja -C build
```

Output: `build/cpu-emulator-<chip>.uf2` (`<chip>` is `RP2350` or
`RP2040`, matching the board), which the build also copies to the
top-level folder as `cpu-emulator-RP2350.uf2` or
`cpu-emulator-RP2040.uf2`. Flash by copying to the `RPI-RP2`
drive — hold BOOTSEL on power-up, or press `~` (SHIFT + backtick) in the
app.

Only the RP2350 build is being kept current while this project is under
active development; the RP2040 build (and a Windows/Linux desktop port,
if one gets added later) will follow once the core design has settled.

## Status

Early development. The memory window with arrow keys and big-square view
is new and not yet tested on real hardware.

## License

MIT — see `LICENSE`. The vendored `picocalc-text-starter-main/` keeps its
own MIT license (Blair Leduc); do not edit it. It is Blair Leduc's code of 2026-10-18 plus a few small local fixes, described below.

The vendored copy is Blair Leduc's `picocalc-text-starter` as it was on 2026-10-18
(commit `85a002e`, "Upgrade to SDK 2.3.1"), with **four small local fixes** that
are not in his repository yet:

1. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/fat32.c`, `fat32_write()` no longer walks
   the cluster chain, allocating a cluster at a cluster-aligned end of file, before
   it allocates the clusters the write needs. That walk could leave a cluster
   unreachable (a leak). A write of zero bytes returns at once.
2. In the same file, `fat32_dir_read()` copies the last part of a long file name of
   248 to 255 characters as far as it fits; upstream drops that part.
3. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/sdcard.c`, a command is not sent to a card
   that is still busy after the 0.5 s wait.
4. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/lcd.c`, `lcd_putstr()` cuts a string off at
   the right edge of the display, because the line buffer holds exactly one row of
   text.

Earlier versions of this copy carried other local changes, and those are now in
the upstream code: the search-hint fix in `get_next_free_cluster()`
([#30](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/30)), the
deleted-entry fixes in `fat32_dir_read()` and `link_entry()`
([#32](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/32)), the timed
busy-card wait in `sdcard.c`
([#33](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/33)) and
`lcd_unblit()` ([#31](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/31)).
`audio.pio` is exactly as downloaded: it now accepts 20 to 20000 Hz
([#29](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/29)), where it used
to accept only 100 to 2000 Hz. Everything else is exactly as downloaded.
